To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Slit and Robos are required to regulate axonal pathfinding in the brain, and that the molecular mechanism regulating Robo/Slits signaling in the brain differs from the molecular mechanisms regulating Slit/Robos signaling in the embryonic nervous system.
the axonal guidance molecules Slit and Robos regulate Drosophila mushroom body development and function, and that Robo3 signaling in mushroom body development is regulated by RPTP69D.
the axonal wiring molecule Robo is regulated by a novel mechanism that is distinct from that of its midline function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of axonal guidance in the Drosophilabrain.
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the development of the nervous system, in particular the development of the central nervous system.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate axonal wiring in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Drosophilla brain is wired by a complex network of signaling molecules, some of which are conserved in vertebrate brain development, and others that are unique to invertebrates, such as the mushroom body.
the Drosophia brain uses a different mechanism to regulate neuronal circuit wiring, partly in response signals from the mushroom bodies.
the Slit-Robo pathway is involved in regulating brain wiring in Drosophila.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain wiring molecule Robo and the axonal wiring molecule Robo are regulated differently in the brain.
Slit and its Robo receptors are conserved axonal guidance molecules, and their signaling pathways are modified in the more complex wiring processes of the Drosophlia brain.
Slit-Robo interactions in the brain are regulated by a novel mechanism involving RPTP69D, and that the mushroom body is a source of Slit for brain wiring.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mechanisms of Robo signaling are modified in higher-order brain wiring.
Robo/Slits signaling mechanisms in the Drosophilia brain have diverged from those in the nerve cord, and that Slit signaling in the brain is not restricted to the midline.
Slit/Robo signaling in the brain is not regulated by midline-derived Slit but rather by mushroom body-derived Slit.
